title: Line sizing and pressure drop
calcLabel: Open the pipe pressure drop calculator

steps.q: Same flow, but the pipe diameter is halved. What happens to the velocity?
steps.title: Velocity
steps.summary: Velocity is flow divided by cross-section area, and area goes with diameter squared. Halving the diameter quarters the area, so the same flow moves four times faster. For reference, 1 m³/h of water in a 25 mm bore pipe flows at about 0.57 m/s.

steps.q: Same flow, diameter halved, turbulent flow. Roughly what happens to the pressure drop?
steps.title: The fifth power
steps.summary: In turbulent flow the friction pressure drop goes with (L/D) × ρv². Velocity goes with 1/D², so v² goes with 1/D⁴, and with the extra 1/D the pressure drop goes roughly with 1/D⁵. Halving the diameter raises it about 2⁵ = 32 times (slightly more in steel pipe, as the friction factor also rises). One pipe size up can cut pressure drop by more than half.

draw: one size up → much less ΔP

steps.q: Typical design velocity for a water line on a pump discharge?
board: for a water line on a pump
steps.title: Rule-of-thumb speeds
steps.summary: Lines are usually sized on a typical velocity and then checked for pressure drop. Rough guides: liquid on a pump discharge about 1.5 to 3 m/s, pump suction about 0.6 to 1.5 m/s to protect NPSH, gravity lines below about 1 m/s, and saturated steam about 20 to 40 m/s.

steps.q: Why is a pump suction line usually one size bigger than the discharge?
board: Why is a pump suction line
steps.title: Suction side
steps.summary: Suction friction reduces NPSH available, so pump suction lines are kept short and usually one size larger than the discharge, with lower velocity. Use an eccentric reducer with the flat side on top at the pump so no vapour pocket forms, and avoid elbows right at the suction nozzle.

draw: no elbow right at the nozzle

steps.q: Steam runs at 25 m/s, water at only 2 m/s. Why can steam go so much faster?
steps.title: Density matters
steps.summary: Pressure drop goes with density × velocity squared. Water is about 1000 kg/m³ while steam at about 7 barg is around 4 kg/m³, so steam at 25 m/s has ρv² of about 2500, similar to water at 2 m/s (about 4000). Steam can therefore run much faster for a similar pressure drop, though too high a velocity causes noise and erosion.

steps.q: A quick-closing valve stops water flowing at 1 m/s in a long line. What happens?
board: m/s in a long line. What
steps.title: Water hammer
steps.summary: Suddenly stopping a long column of moving liquid converts its momentum into a pressure surge: water hammer. The rise is about density × pressure-wave speed × change in velocity, roughly 13 bar for each 1 m/s of water stopped in a steel line, on top of the normal pressure. It can burst gaskets and jump pipes off supports, so close valves slowly on long liquid lines, or check the surge where a valve must shut fast.

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today: pipes. Pick the wrong size and you pay for it every day. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Now size your own line in the pipe pressure drop calculator.

q1.text: Question 1. Same flow, but the pipe diameter is halved. What happens to the velocity?

q1-r0.text: Doubles? You forgot the area is a circle. Square it.

q1-r1.text: 4 times. Area goes with diameter squared. Correct!

q1-r2.text: Halves? Same flow through a smaller hole goes faster, not slower.

q1-r3.text: The same flow has to squeeze through a quarter of the area.

q1-b0.text: Velocity is flow divided by the pipe's cross-section area.

q1-b1.text: Area goes with diameter squared. Half the diameter, a quarter of the area.

q1-b2.text: So the same flow through half the diameter moves four times faster.

q1-b3.text: Handy rule for water: one cubic metre an hour in a 25 millimetre bore pipe is a little over half a metre per second.

q2.text: Question 2. Same flow, diameter halved, turbulent flow. Roughly what happens to the pressure drop?

q2-r0.text: If only. Pressure drop is far more sensitive than that.

q2-r1.text: That's just the velocity. Friction gets worse faster.

q2-r2.text: About 30 times! Diameter to the fifth. Painful, right?

q2-r3.text: Too much. It's bad, but not quite that bad.

q2-b0.text: Friction loss goes with length over diameter, times velocity squared.

q2-b1.text: Velocity goes with one over D squared, so v squared goes with one over D to the fourth. Then one more D from L over D.

q2-b2.text: Two to the fifth is 32. In steel pipe the friction factor rises a little too, so call it 30 times or a bit more.

q2-b3.text: Going one pipe size up can cut pressure drop by more than half. Worth checking before you buy a bigger pump.

q3.text: Question 3. Typical design velocity for a water line on a pump discharge?

q3-r0.text: 0.1? That pipe would be the size of a culvert.

q3-r2.text: 10 metres per second of water? Erosion and hammer, here we come.

q3-r3.text: 30 is for steam. Water would shake the pipe rack apart.

q3-b0.text: Most plants size lines on velocity first, then check the pressure drop.

q3-b1.text: Liquid on a pump discharge: about 1.5 to 3 metres per second.

q3-b2.text: Pump suction: slower, about 0.6 to 1.5, to protect the NPSH.

q3-b3.text: Gravity lines run even slower. Saturated steam, being light, runs at 20 to 40 metres per second.

q4.text: Question 4. Why is a pump suction line usually one size bigger than the discharge?

q4-r0.text: Looks? The pump doesn't care what you think of the piping.

q4-r1.text: Yes! Every bit of suction friction comes out of NPSH.

q4-r2.text: Suction is the low-pressure side. That's the whole point.

q4-r3.text: Bigger pipe costs more, not less. There's a better reason.

q4-b0.text: Suction friction is a withdrawal from the NPSH available.

q4-b1.text: A bigger, shorter suction line means slower liquid and less friction, so more NPSH is left at the impeller eye.

q4-b2.text: Use an eccentric reducer at the pump, flat side on top, so no vapour pocket forms.

q4-b3.text: And keep elbows away from the suction nozzle, so the flow arrives smooth.

q5.text: Question 5. Steam runs at 25 m/s, water at only 2 m/s. Why can steam go so much faster?

q5-r0.text: Same steel, same schedule. Strength isn't the reason.

q5-r1.text: Right! Pressure drop goes with density times v squared.

q5-r2.text: No friction? Steam lines would love that. Not true.

q5-r3.text: Steam headers run all over the plant. Not short.

q5-b0.text: Pressure drop goes with density times velocity squared.

q5-b1.text: Water is about 1000 kilograms per cubic metre. Steam at about 7 bar gauge is around 4.

q5-b2.text: So steam at 25 has a rho v squared of about 2500. Water at 2 is about 4000. Similar, even though steam is twelve times faster.

q5-b3.text: Too fast is still bad for steam: noise, erosion and wet steam hitting bends. Stay in the normal range.

q6.text: Question 6. A quick-closing valve stops water flowing at 1 m/s in a long line. What happens?

q6-r0.text: Nearly incompressible, so the pressure has nowhere to go but up.

q6-r2.text: The pump doesn't speed up. The pipe takes the hit.

q6-r3.text: Empties? The liquid slams to a stop, it doesn't vanish.

q6-b0.text: Stop a long column of moving water suddenly, and its momentum turns into pressure.

q6-b1.text: The rise is density times wave speed times the change in velocity. For water, about 13 bar for every metre per second stopped.

q6-b2.text: That's on top of the normal pressure, and it can burst gaskets and jump pipes off supports.

q6-b3.text: Close valves slowly on long liquid lines, or check the surge if a valve must shut fast. Check your own line in the pipe pressure drop calculator on pharmacheme dot in.
